InstanceRefer: Cooperative Holistic Understanding for Visual Grounding on Point Clouds through Instance Multi-level Contextual Referring

Zhihao Yuan†    Xu Yan†    Yinghong Liao    Ruimao Zhang    Zhen Li    and Shuguang Cui

The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen) ††thanks: Corresponding author: Zhen Li. $ˆ†$ Equal first authorship.    Shenzhen Research Institute of Big Data
{zhihaoyuan@, xuyan1@link., lizhen@}cuhk.edu.cn
Abstract

Compared with the visual grounding in 2D images, the natural-language-guided 3D object localization on point clouds is more challenging due to the sparse and disordered property. In this paper, we propose a new model, named InstanceRefer11 1 https://github.com/CurryYuan/InstanceRefer, to achieve a superior 3D visual grounding through unifying instance attribute, relation and localization perceptions. In practice, based on the predicted target category from natural language, our model first filters instances from panoptic segmentation on point clouds to obtain a small number of candidates. Note that such instance-level candidates are more effective and rational than the redundant 3D object-proposal candidates. Then, for each candidate, we conduct the cooperative holistic scene-language understanding, i.e., multi-level contextual referring from instance attribute perception, instance-to-instance relation perception and instance-to-background global localization perception. Eventually, the most relevant candidate is localized effectively through adaptive confidence fusion. Experiments confirm that our InstanceRefer outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by a large margin, i.e., 9.5% improvement on the ScanRefer benchmark (ranked 1st place) and 7.2% improvement on Sr3D.

1 Introduction

Visual Grounding (VG) has received various attention and achieved great progress in recent years [17, 25, 37, 23, 26]. Given vision input and the related language query, VG aims to locate the desired objects or regions in the input, which usually requires a high-level visual and linguistic holistic understanding. Benefiting from the regular grid of 2D images, the dense object detector ( \ie object-aware bounding boxes ) are widely exploited by traditional 2D visual grounding models to refer the corresponding objects based on the textual descriptions. However, such a 2D-based scheme is usually deficient in depicting real scenarios due to object occlusions and ambiguous semantic relations.

With the rapid development of 3D sensor and 3D representation, VG task has gradually merged more informative 3D data. For example, by using point clouds as 3D raw data, VG task spawns and boosts various 3D visual applications [3, 36], \egrobotic perception and indoor navigation. In literature, Chen et al [4] is the pioneer for 3D visual grounding, which proposes the ScanRefer dataset and formulates the 3D VG task as a grounding-by-detection problem. In practice, it first uses the state-of-the-art detector (\ieVoteNet [31]) to generate proposals, where features of each proposal are concatenated with a global representation of the linguistic query to form a fused feature. Then, such fused features are directly leveraged to predict the proposal with the largest confident score. However, it is still suffering from several issues while extending 2D VG to 3D VG as follows. (1) The object proposals in the large 3D scene are usually redundant. Compared with the actual instances, proposal quantity is large and the inter-proposals relationship is complex, which inevitably introduces the difficulties and noises. (2) The appearance and attribution information are not fully captured. Due to the noise or occlusion, the acquired point cloud is usually sparse and incomplete, leading to missing geometric details in object-aware proposals. Conventional point cloud-based methods fails to extract the appearance and attribution information, \egred, gray and wooden, which usually misses the vital linguistic cue for referring. (3) No explicit and interpretable cue is provided for referring. Due to the long description in ScanRefer dataset [4], it is non-trivial to build an entire scene graph. Thus, ScanRefer [4] selects the most relevant proposal directly through the fused visual feature and linguistic features matching. In this manner, the relationships between proposals and with the background are not fully studied.

To address the above issues, in this work, we investigate a novel framework, namely InstanceRefer, and reformulate 3D VG on point clouds as an instance-matching problem. Specifically, through the global panoptic segmentation by any appealing models, several instances sub-point clouds are extracted from the original large scene. Compared with object-proposal based candidates, these instance sub-point clouds appeal to some more original geometric details with attributes (\iecolor, texture, \etc). After that, these instances are filtered by the predicted category from natural language description, obtaining the set of candidates. In this way, we not only reduce greatly the quantity of the candidates, but also maintain the original information for each candidate without extra interference from overlapped objects. Besides, multi-level contextual learning modules (see Fig. 1) are proposed to explicitly capture the context of each candidate from instance attribute, instance-to-instance relationship, and instance-to-background global localization, fully understanding the whole scene. Eventually, we conduct the visual guided linguistic attention for cooperative holistic scene-text understanding, where visual-linguistic features are adaptively matched and fused for grounding.

In summary, the key contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) We propose a new framework InstanceRefer for visual grounding on point clouds. Specifically, we innovatively exploit panoptic segmentation and language cues to select the instance sub-point clouds as candidates, reformulating it as an instance-matching problem. (2) Three novel components are proposed to select the most relevant instance candidate from attributes, local relationships and global localization aspects jointly. (3) Extensive experiments on ScanRefer dataset confirm that the efficiency of InstanceRefer, achieving 10% improvement for overall accuracy. Furthremore, to verify our proposed modules’ effectiveness, we validate AP and RP modules on ReferIt3D dataset and achieve 7% improvement.

2 Related Work

Visual Grounding on 2D Images. The task of visual grounding is to localize a specific region of the image described by a natural language query. Depending on the type of language query, it can be further divided into phrase localization [17, 30, 37] and referring expression comprehension [27, 21, 38]. Most approaches conduct localization in the bounding box level and separate the VG with two stages. The first stage is to generate candidate proposals with either unsupervised methods or a pre-trained object detection network. In the second stage, the best matching proposal is selected according to the language query. Such two-stage methods focus on improving the ranking accuracy of the second stage. For instance, MAttNet [45] proposes a modular attention network to decompose the language query to different components and process them in different modular networks separately. Many recent works [24, 43, 22] use scene graphs [16] to extract more precisely the entities and relations from the referring expression. However, they heavily rely on the quality of the converted scene graph. The referring language in ScanRefer is much complicated and comprised of multiple sentences. Thus it is difficult to parse the whole description without scene graph ground-truths. Thus, we do not exploit the explicit entire scene graph in our task.

Visual Grounding on 3D Point Clouds. Chen et al [4] released a new dataset for visual grounding on 3D point clouds. Their proposed network, ScanRefer, merges the state-of-the-art detection framework with a language encoder in a joint-learning strategy. Specifically, through the deep Hough-voting network [31], hundreds of object proposals are generated to interact with language features. After that, a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) uses concatenated features from proposals and language to generate a final score for each proposal. Eventually, the most relevant proposal is selected by ranking all the scores. However, such a simple baseline method neither provides an explicit interpretable module for grounding cues nor considers the noise brought by the redundant object proposals.

3D Representation Learning on Point Clouds. Point clouds are sparsely-scattered, thus cannot be represented like regular-aligned 2D image pixels. How to effectively handle and utilize point cloud information has been a big challenge in 3D research. To address this issue, two main strategies have been proposed: voxel-based and point-based. (1) Due to point cloud data’s sparse and memory-consuming properties, traditional 3D methods of voxelization and 3D convolution are ineffective in learning point cloud features. A variety of works has been presented for improvement in recent years, including more efficient spatial sparse convolution [5, 9] and octree-based convolutional neural networks [39, 34]. (2) Point-based models leverage the permutation invariant nature of raw point cloud for enhanced 3D processing [32, 33]. Specifically, most point-based models first sample sub-points from the initial point clouds, then apply feature aggregation function on each sub-point in a local point cloud cluster after the grouping. The representatives of the point-based methods are graph-based learning [41, 47, 20, 19] and convolution-like operations [14, 8, 46, 40, 35, 42, 12]. With the development of the representation learning on point clouds, various downstream tasks related to VG on point clouds have been explored rapidly, e.g., 3D object detection [31] and instance segmentation [15].

3 Method

This section presents the methodology of our proposed framework, InstanceRefer, for visual grounding on point clouds, including the details of the model architecture and the objective function applied in model training.

3.1 Overview

Our proposed InstanceRefer is a novel framework for point cloud visual grounding, which conducts the multi-level contextual referring to match the most relevant instance-level candidate. In practice, as shown in Fig. 2, by exploiting point cloud panoptic segmentation, InstanceRefer first extracts instances with their semantic labels from the whole scene (Sec. 3.2). Following that, the input text is embedded into high-dimensional feature space, and a target category classification is conducted as the linguistic guidance (Sec. 3.3). Finally, after filtering out the candidates from all instances, the three-level progressive referring modules, \ieattribute perception (AP) module, relation perception (RP) module, and global localization perception (GLP) module (Sec. 3.4), are employed to select the optimal candidate.

3.2 Instance Set Generation

Unlike ScanRefer that selects the candidates from all object-proposals [4], our framework first extracts all MM foreground instances from the input point cloud to generate an instance set. Then, it reformulates the 3D visual grounding problem as an instance matching problem.

For this purpose, panoptic segmentation [18] is adopted innovatively in our model, which aims to tackle the semantic segmentation and the instance segmentation jointly. Specifically, PointGroup [15] is used as the backbone. Taking a point cloud P∈ℝN×3P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} and its features F∈ℝN×DF\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} (\egRGB or extra normal vector) as inputs, InstanceRefer returns two prediction sets (\iethe semantics segmentation mask SS and the instance mask II). Furthermore, S∈ℝN×1S\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1} records the predicted semantic labels for each point, and the instance mask I∈ℝN×1I\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1} saves the instance indices. The semantic label of each point in the point cloud is within the total CC categories. The instance index is less than the total instance number MM in the scene. Therefore, InstanceRefer selects the mm-th instance from the point cloud by

PmI={pi,∀pi∈P,∀ii∈I s.t. ii=m},\displaystyle P^{I}_{m}=\{p_{i},~\forall p_{i}\in P,~\forall i_{i}\in I~\text{ s.t. }~i_{i}=m\}, (1)

where PmIP^{I}_{m} denotes the point cloud of mm-th instance, and ii∈Ii_{i}\in I is the instance mask of the ii-th point. Overall, the point clouds of all foreground instances are represented as 𝑷I={PmI}m=0M\boldsymbol{P}^{I}=\{P^{I}_{m}\}_{m=0}^{M}. Similarly, features and semantics of all instances are denoted as 𝑭I\boldsymbol{F}^{I} and 𝑺I\boldsymbol{S}^{I}, respectively.

3.3 Description Encoding

The input query description is first tokenized into words by SpaCy [11] and further mapped into a sequence of vectors W={wi}∈RNw×300W=\{w_{i}\}\in R^{N_{w}\times 300} via the pre-trained GloVe word embeddings [29]. The sequences of embedding vectors WW are then fed into two Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) [6] layers that perform as the textual encoder E={ei}∈RNw×DE=\{e_{i}\}\in R^{N_{w}\times D}. Based on the visual guidance from different aspects, InstanceRefer employs attention pooling to automatically generate individual language encoders accordingly through optimized joint self-attention. In practice, given the features of each token ei∈Ee_{i}\in E, the attention pooling updates the features by

e^i\displaystyle\hat{e}_{i} =𝒜{ℛ(ei,ej)wj,∀ej∈E,wj∈W},\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}\{\mathcal{R}(e_{i},e_{j})w_{j},~~\forall e_{j}\in E,~~w_{j}\in W\}, (2)
E^\displaystyle\hat{E} =𝒜​{e^i}i=0NW,\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}\{\hat{e}_{i}\}_{i=0}^{N_{W}}, (3)

where the aggregation function 𝒜\mathcal{A} is set as max pooling and a pairwise relationship function ℛ\mathcal{R} are normalized dot-product similarity between features of two tokens. The features of each token ei∈Ee_{i}\in E are then updated to e^i\hat{e}_{i} by the aggregation of all token features weighted by relation. The global representation of the query is represented as E^∈ℝ1×D\hat{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times D}. InstanceRefer leverages three independent parallel attention pooling layers since the model has three downstream modules (\ieAP, RP, and GLP modules), and the output features are denoted as E^A\hat{E}^{A}, E^R\hat{E}^{R} and E^G\hat{E}^{G}, respectively. Furthermore, by appending an additional GRU layer, InstanceRefer predicts the target category SES^{E} of the query by language features EE. This output aids the model in subsequently filtering out the candidates from MM instances.

3.4 Linguistic Guided Multi-Level Visual Context

Before feeding the instances into the following modules, InstanceRefer first uses the predicted target category from the previous language encoder to obtain the potential candidates. In formula, by taking the predicted category of the description SES^{E} and the semantic mask 𝑺I\boldsymbol{S}^{I} for instances, the model obtains the candidate set 𝑷^I\hat{\boldsymbol{P}}^{I} by

P^I={PiI,∀PiI∈PI,∀SiI∈𝑺I s.t. SiI=SE}.\displaystyle\hat{P}^{I}=\{{P}^{I}_{i},~\forall{P}^{I}_{i}\in{P}^{I},~\forall{S}^{I}_{i}\in{\boldsymbol{S}}^{I}~\text{ s.t. }~{S}^{I}_{i}=S^{E}\}. (4)

Similarly, the corresponding features of candidates 𝑭^I\hat{\boldsymbol{F}}^{I} are attained. In practice, the accuracy of target classification on the query can achieve over 97%. Hence the above filter will not introduce any obvious noise for further referring. Then, the features of each candidate in a multi-level manner with three downstream modules are extracted as follows:
AP Module. Considering there could be many adjectives in a sentence, \eg”a long bookshelf” for scale, ”a brown chair” for color, ”a square table” for shape \etc, for attribute descriptions, an attribute perception (AP) module is designed to explicitly capture such information. Concretely, the AP module takes the information of the ii-th candidate (\iepoint cloud P^iI\hat{P}^{I}_{i} and its attribute features F^iI\hat{F}^{I}_{i}) as input and generates a global representation vector FiAF^{A}_{i} of the candidate. As shown in Fig. 3 (a), our model constructs a four-layer feature extractor with Sparse Convolution (SparseConv) [10]. The extractor firstly voxelizes the point cloud into 3D voxels and then conducts the convolution operation only on non-empty voxels in a more efficient way. Note that here the normal point-based network (\egPointNet++ [33]) is not adopted since they are generally insensitive to color information. Subsequently, by conducting an average pooling, the features representation F^A∈ℝ1×D\hat{F}^{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times D} is obtained.

RP Module. Since there are many descriptions about the relation between different instances (\eg”The desk is between the black chair and bed”), using only the attribute-related manner fails to capture such information. Therefore, a relation perception (RP) module is proposed for the relation encoding between the candidate and its surrounding instances. Fig. 3 (b) illustrates the design of the RP module. In practice, given the ii-th candidate point cloud P^iI\hat{P}^{I}_{i}, the RP module firstly searches KK instance-level neighborhoods that have the closest Euclidean distance to the center of instance P^iI\hat{P}^{I}_{i}. Following that, a graph-based aggregation is employed to fuse the features of local neighborhoods. To define the edge-relation ri​j{r}_{ij} between the ii-th candidate and the kk-th neighboring instance, the RP module adopts the DGCNN [41] as follows:

ri​k=σ1​{[avg​(P^iI)−avg​(PkI),ℋ⁡(SiE),ℋ⁡(SkI)]},{r}_{ik}=\sigma_{1}\{[\text{avg}(\hat{P}^{I}_{i})-\text{avg}({P}^{I}_{k}),\mathcal{H}(S^{E}_{i}),\mathcal{H}(S^{I}_{k})]\}, (5)

where avg​(⋅)\text{avg}(\cdot) and ℋ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{H}(\cdot) are global points average pooling and one-hot encoding, respectively. The sign [⋅,⋅][\cdot,\cdot] means the channel-wise concatenation. The sign σ\sigma is the share-weighted multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). Through Eq. (5), the RP module considers not only the relative position but also the semantic relationship between the candidate and its neighbors. Eventually, the enhanced feature F^iR∈ℝ1×D\hat{F}^{R}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times D} for the ii-th candidate can be obtained by

F^iR=𝒜{ri​k∗σ2([PkI,SkI]),∀PkI∈𝒩(P^iI,K)},\hat{F}^{R}_{i}=\mathcal{A}\{{r}_{ik}*\sigma_{2}([{P}^{I}_{k},S^{I}_{k}]),~\forall{P}^{I}_{k}\in\mathcal{N}(\hat{P}^{I}_{i},K)\}, (6)

where 𝒩⁡(P^iI,K)\mathcal{N}(\hat{P}^{I}_{i},K) denotes the KK nearest neighboring instances for P^iI\hat{P}^{I}_{i} and the sign ∗* represents the element-wise multiplication. Note that the MLPs σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} have the same output dimensions.
GLP Module. The global localization perception (GLP) module aims to supplement the background information neglected by the two aforementioned modules. There are other descriptions about global localization information, (\eg”in the corner” and ”next to the wall”), but such information cannot be included in the AP and RP modules. As shown in Fig. 4, the GLP module takes the entire point cloud as input. By applying another SparseConv encoder, the module first extracts the point-wise features of the entire scene. An average pooling in the height axis is then performed to generate the bird-eyes-view (BEV) features. Here, each input point cloud is divided into 3×33\times 3 areas in the BEV plane. By repeatedly concatenating the language features E^G\hat{E}^{G} and then flowing through the MLPs, the GLP module predicts the object candidate’s location in one of the nine areas. Moreover, the probability of each area is interpolated into the point cloud of the ii-th candidate P^iI\hat{P}^{I}_{i} by

f^i,kB\displaystyle\hat{f}^{B}_{i,k} =∑j=1nωj​Ajprob,ωj=1(p^i,kI−Ajcent)2,\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\omega_{j}A^{\text{prob}}_{j},~~~\omega_{j}=\frac{1}{(\hat{p}^{I}_{i,k}-A^{\text{cent}}_{j})^{2}}, (7)

where n=9n=9 represents the total number of areas, AjprobA^{\text{prob}}_{j} and AjcentA^{\text{cent}}_{j} are the probabilities of localization and center coordinates of jj-th area in the total nine areas, respectively. p^i,kI∈P^iI\hat{p}^{I}_{i,k}\in\hat{P}^{I}_{i} and f^i,kB\hat{f}^{B}_{i,k} are the coordinate and interpolated features of the kk-th point in the ii-th candidate. Finally, after concatenating interpolated features with candidate features, another attention pooling (Eq. (3)) aggregates the features of the ii-th candidate to a global representation F^iG\hat{F}_{i}^{G}.

3.5 Candidate Matching and Objective Function

With the multi-level visual features of the candidates (\ieF^A\hat{F}^{A}, F^R\hat{F}^{R} and F^G\hat{F}^{G}) and the language features obtained through corresponding attention pooling (\ieE^A\hat{E}^{A}, E^R\hat{E}^{R} and E^G\hat{E}^{G}), InstanceRefer conducts a matching process at different levels. Take the features from AP module as an example. For the ii-th candidate, the model generates a similarity score between its features F^iA\hat{F}^{A}_{i} and the language features E^A\hat{E}^{A} via

QiA=cos⁡(F^iA,E^A)=F^iA⋅E^A‖F^iA‖​‖E^A‖.{Q}^{A}_{i}=\cos(\hat{F}^{A}_{i},\hat{E}^{A})=\frac{\hat{F}^{A}_{i}\cdot\hat{E}^{A}}{||\hat{F}^{A}_{i}||||\hat{E}^{A}||}. (8)

The scores for RP QiR{Q}^{R}_{i} and GLP QiG{Q}^{G}_{i} can be obtained by using the same method. After that, our framework weighted-average the three scores for the candidate with the weights learned from a single linear layer. Finally, the candidate with the highest score is selected as the final output.

For the objective function, our model adopts a contrastive manner to optimize this solution. Here the candidate object with the largest overlap with the GT object bounding box is set as the positive candidate while others are regarded as negative ones. If the largest IoU of candidates is below the threshold of 0.2, the loss computation does not include that of the relevant query. Furthermore, the similarity in positive pairs should be higher than that in negative pairs by a margin of Γ\Gamma. For this purpose, the scores of positive and all negative candidates, denoted as Q+Q^{+} and Q−={Qi}i=0M′Q^{-}=\{Q_{i}\}_{i=0}^{M^{\prime}}, are collected, where M′M^{\prime} is the number of negative candidates in the scene. All negative candidates are taken into the optimization process, where the most negative one produces the largest loss and favors the convergence

Lcons=∑Q−max⁡(Γ−Q++Q−,0).L_{\text{cons}}=\sum_{Q^{-}}\max(\Gamma-Q^{+}+Q^{-},0). (9)

Language classification loss LclsL_{\text{cls}} and BEV localization loss LbevL_{\text{bev}} are also included for joint target categorization and localization prediction. The final loss is a linear combination of the contrastive loss, the language to object classification loss, and localization loss. L=Lcons+λ1​Lcls+λ2​LbevL=L_{\text{cons}}+\lambda_{1}L_{\text{cls}}+\lambda_{2}L_{\text{bev}}, where λ1=λ2=0.1\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=0.1 are the weights to adjust the ratios of each loss, respectively.

4 Experiments

In this section, we present the experimental procedure and analysis in detail to demonstrate the effectiveness of our InstanceRefer in 3D Visual Grounding.

4.1 Implementation

In our experiment, we use the official pre-trained PointGroup [15] as the backbone to perform the panoptic segmentation. For language encoding, we employ the same GloVE and BiGRU used in ScanRefer [4] to generate the word features in channel D=256D=256. The output of each attention pooling preserves the identical 256 channels. The AP module consists of four 3D sparse convolution blocks, each of which has two 3D sparse convolutions inside. Going deeper, we gradually increase the number of channels (\ie32, 64, 128, 256). The GLP module applies the same structure of the sparse convolution block but with fewer blocks (\ie3 blocks with channel 32, 128, 256). In the RP module, the kNN instance number KK is 8, and the channel numbers of MLPs σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} are (256,256) and (256), respectively.

Since our framework employs a pre-trained panoptic segmentation model and stores the segmentation results offline, the training time is much shorter than that of ScanRefer. We train the network for 20 epochs by using the Adam optimizer with the batch size of 128. The learning rate of the network is initialized as 0.001 with the decay as 0.9 for every 10 epochs. All experiments are implemented on PyTorch and a single NVIDIA 1080Ti GPU.

4.2 Dataset and Metrics

Extensive experiments are firstly conducted on the ScanRefer dataset, the sole 3D point cloud visual grounding dataset that exists, to the best of our knowledge. Specifically, the ScanRefer dataset contains 51,538 descriptions for ScanNet scenes [7]. The dataset is split into 36,655 samples for training, 9,508 samples for validation, and 5,410 samples for testing, respectively. Furthremore, to verify our proposed modules’ effectiveness, we validate AP and RP modules on Sr3D and Nr3D datases (proposed in ReferIt3D [2]), which use the same train/valid split with ScanRefer on ScanNet but exploit manually extracted instances as inputs. Specifically, Sr3D (Spatial Reference in 3D) contains 83.5K synthetic expressions generated by a simple composition template and Nr3D (Natural Reference in 3D) has 41.5K human expressions collected as ReferItGame [17]. Both datasets aim to ground a natural language expression to an object in the 3D scene. Since it directly uses point clouds of instances as inputs, it can be seen as the instance-matching stage of our InstanceRefer without interaction with the environment (i.e., GLP module with wall and floor).

For the ScanRefer dataset, InstanceRefer calculates the 3D intersection over union (IoU) between the predicted bounding box and ground truth. The Acc@mmIoU is adopted as the evaluation metric, where m∈[0.25,0.5]m\in[0.25,0.5]. Accuracy is reported on ”unique” and ”multiple” categories, respectively. If there is only a single object of its class in the scene, we take it as ”unique”, otherwise ”multiple”. Moreover, to fully evaluate our model, we conduct a fair comparison on both the validation set and the benchmark22 2 http://kaldir.vc.in.tum.de/scanrefer_benchmark, and strictly control the input modality (\ie2D and 3D). For Sr3D/Nr3D datasets, we use the same strategies and metrics in their official paper and compare results in different levels.

4.3 Quantitative Comparisons

To fully evaluate the proposed IntanceRefer, we compared our method with previous methods on the ScanRefer dataset. The results of SCRC [13], One-stage [44] and ScanRefer [4] are shown in Tab. 1. Among them, since SCRC [13] and One-stage [44] are 2D based methods, we depict their modality as ”2D only”. They are trained by using the annotation of the recorded scan video with the closest camera pose, and predict the target 2D bounding boxes in each frame. Then they select the 2D bounding box with the highest confidence score and project it to 3D location using the depth map of that frame. ScanRefer is the current state-of-the-art method that takes coordinates, RGB information, and normals of point clouds as input (”3D only”). To further improve the performance, they also project the multi-view image features from the pre-trained ENet [28] to the point cloud. We denote such modality as ”2D and 3D”.

As shown in Tab. 1, it is obvious that our model gains the highest scores on both the validation set and the testing set. Note that 2D based methods (SCRC and One-stage) cannot achieve satisfactory results since they are limited by the view of a single frame. Among ”3D only” methods, InstanceRefer achieves the best performance on all metrics. Specifically, our method achieves a remarkable ∼\sim28% improvement of Acc@0.25 in ”unique” case and ∼\sim6% in ”multiple” on the validation set, which mainly comes from our well-designed pipeline and three novel modules. More importantly, even if ScanRefer uses 2D information (”2D and 3D”), the overall result of our ”3D only” can still achieve ∼\sim9% in Acc@0.25. Furthermore, our results on online benchmark are also much higher than theirs, and these results hold with or without the auxiliary 2D information.

The results in Tab. 2 illustrates the instance-matching accuracy on Nr3D and Sr3D datasets. The results surprisingly show that our InstanceRefer achieves 38.8% on Nr3D (labeled by human) and 48.0% on Sr3D (labeled by machine), which are 3.2% and 8.2% higher than ReferIt3DNet. The experiment proves that our proposed perception modules can be the effective components for accurate grounding on scenes of point clouds and enhance the pure instance-matching performance, thus outperforming ScanRefer for 3D VG on point clouds.

Visualization results produced by ScanRefer and by our method are displayed in Fig. 5. Predicted boxes are marked green if they have an IoU score higher than 0.5, otherwise, they are marked red. Failure cases of ScanRefer indicate that its architecture cannot handle spatial relations to distinguish ambiguous objects. On the contrary, InstanceRefer can accurately localize the described object even in very complex scenarios with long textual descriptions (\egthe first and second columns).

4.4 Ablation Studies

This subsection further discusses the effects of each designed modules and input in our model.

Design analysis. The upper part of Tab. 3 shows the results of different module combinations in the model. On one hand, if only one single perception module is used, the AP module can achieve the best result. On the other hand, when additional RP and GLP modules are used, there is a remarkable improvement over the AP module’s result. Specifically, the improvement of the RP module is slightly larger than that of the GLP module. This is mainly because the descriptions of the correlation among instances in the scene are more commonly compared with the localization.

Different inputs. The lower part of the Tab. 3 presents the result of different inputs. Specifically, when the color and normal information are not used, there is only a slight drop in our result, proving that our model is robust for input variants and has outstanding ability in seizing features. Furthermore, we investigate the situation that our model uses ground truth instances or ground truths of target category prediction. When GT instances are appended, there is a huge improvement of 24% on overall Acc@0.5. These results show that if InstanceRefer uses a stronger panoptic segmentation backbone, there is still a large room for improvement. However, if our framework uses GT language classification (GT lang cls), the improvement is limited. The reason is that the language classification results achieve an accuracy that is higher than 97%.

4.5 Comprehensive Analysis

Advantage of panoptic segmentation. We compare the matching difficulty using the accurate candidate from detection or panoptic segmentation in Tab. 4. From the predicted object proposals of the VoteNet [31], InstanceRefer arbitrarily selects one bounding box proposals with the correct semantic class label (denoted as VoteNetRand). When panoptic segmentation (PanoSegRand) is applied, there is a huge improvement for random selection. At the same time, panoptic segmentation preserves the original geometric information of an instance.

Visualization results of attention. We illustrate the visualization results of attention pooling in Fig. 6. For different token, three modules give different attention. It is evident that InstanceRefer attends to the desired phrases in the sentence. Specifically, the RP module focuses on the reference object boxes that aids the model in locating the expected target bookshelves. GLP module highlights the words about the global position, \iecorner, to accurately identify where the target bookshelves locates. In the query, the phrase we are looking for is the attribute of the object bookshelves, and the AP module pays attention to it accordingly. More details will be shown in the supplementary.

Robustness for incomplete description. The results of ScanRefer and InstanceRefer when using different input lengths are presented in Tab. 5. Thanks to the multi-level referring strategy, our method is also very robust for incomplete language inputs.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we proposed a novel framework, named InstanceRefer, for 3D visual grounding. It achieves more accurate localization via unifying instance attribute, relation, and localization perceptions. Specifically, our framework innovatively predicts the target category from natural language and filters out a small number of candidates by panoptic segmentation. Moreover, we propose the concept of cooperative holistic scene-language understanding for each candidate, i.e., multi-level contextual referring to instance attribute, instance-to-instance relation, and instance-to-background global localization. Experimental results and analysis demonstrate that our InstanceRefer outperforms previous methods by a large margin. We believe our work formulates a new strategy for future 3D VG.
